# Constitution of India: Education Articles, Schedules, Amendments and Delhi's Status

> **What UPSC asks on this**
> 1. "Which Amendment inserted or moved X?" The 86th gave Art 21A; the 42nd moved education to the Concurrent List; the 7th gave Art 350A and 350B; the 93rd gave Art 15(5); the 44th gave Art 30(1A).
> 2. Statement sets on Art 21A, Art 45 and Art 51A(k): the age band, the Part they sit in, who is bound, whether a court can enforce them, and the date they came into force.
> 3. Match-the-following on Articles 28, 29, 30, 41, 45, 46, 47 and 350A.
> 4. Seventh Schedule: Entry 25 of List III versus Entry 66 of List I, and the five subjects the 42nd Amendment shifted.
> 5. Landmark cases in order: Mohini Jain, Unni Krishnan, T.M.A. Pai, Inamdar, Society for Unaided Private Schools, Pramati.
> 6. Delhi's constitutional position: Art 239AA, the 69th and 70th Amendments, 70 MLAs, 7 ministers, and the three excluded subjects.

## 1. The map: where education sits in the Constitution

**Education appears in four places: Part III rights, Part IV directives, Part IVA duties and the Seventh Schedule lists.** Knowing which Part an Article belongs to answers half the statement questions, because the Part decides whether a court can enforce it.

- **Part III (Art 12 to 35), Fundamental Rights**: enforceable by courts. Education Articles here are **21A, 28, 29, 30** and the equality clauses **15(3), 15(4), 15(5), 15(6)**.
- **Part IV (Art 36 to 51), Directive Principles**: **not enforceable by any court (Art 37)**, but fundamental in governance. Education directives are **Art 41, 45, 46**, with **39(e), 39(f)** and **47** on children's health.
- **Part IVA (Art 51A), Fundamental Duties**: eleven duties; **51A(k)** binds the parent or guardian.
- **Seventh Schedule**: decides who may legislate. **Entry 25 of List III (Concurrent)** is "Education"; **Entries 63 to 66 of List I (Union)** cover institutions of national importance and standards in higher education.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C[Constitution of India] --> P3[Part III Fundamental Rights]
  C --> P4[Part IV Directive Principles]
  C --> P4A[Part IVA Fundamental Duties]
  C --> S7[Seventh Schedule Lists]
  P3 --> A21[Art 21A, 28, 29, 30]
  P4 --> A45[Art 41, 45, 46]
  P4A --> A51[Art 51A k parent duty]
  S7 --> E25[Entry 25 Concurrent List]
```

## 2. Basics the paper still tests

**Dates, counts and names from the making of the Constitution come as one or two easy marks.**

- Constituent Assembly first met **9 December 1946**. Drafting Committee chair: **Dr B.R. Ambedkar**. Constitution adopted **26 November 1949** (Constitution Day), in force **26 January 1950**.
- Originally **395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules**. Today **12 Schedules** and **25 Parts** (Parts IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA were added; Part VII was repealed by the 7th Amendment).
- The Preamble has been amended **once**, by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**, adding "socialist", "secular" and "integrity".
- **Art 32** is the right to constitutional remedies, called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution by Ambedkar. It can be used only to enforce Fundamental Rights. **Art 226** gives High Courts a wider writ power, usable "for any other purpose" too, that is, for ordinary legal rights as well. A Delhi government teacher with a routine service grievance, such as an illegal termination order, does not go straight to the Supreme Court under Art 32. The case goes first to the **Central Administrative Tribunal**, and its order can then be challenged in the Delhi High Court under Art 226 (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).

## 3. Fundamental Rights that reach the school gate

**About a dozen Articles of Part III deal with admissions, fees, religion in school, minority schools and child labour.**

**Equality (Art 14, 15, 16).** Art 14 gives equality before law; Mohini Jain (1992) used it to strike down capitation fees. **Art 15(3)** lets the State make special provisions for women and children, which is the constitutional basis for girls' hostels and the Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas. **Art 15(4)** was added by the **1st Amendment, 1951** after the Champakam Dorairajan case struck down a Madras communal admission order. It lets the State make special provision for socially and educationally backward classes and SC/ST. **Art 15(5)**, added by the **93rd Amendment, 2005** (in force **20 January 2006**), extends this to admission in **private educational institutions, aided or unaided, except minority institutions** under Art 30(1). **Art 15(6) and 16(6)**, added by the **103rd Amendment, 2019**, allow up to **10 per cent for Economically Weaker Sections**; the Supreme Court upheld them in **Janhit Abhiyan (2022)** by a 3:2 majority.

**Art 19(1)(g).** Running a school is an "occupation". In **T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002, 11 judges)** the Supreme Court held:
- all citizens may establish educational institutions under Art 19(1)(g);
- minorities have the additional protection of Art 30(1);
- capitation fees and profiteering are barred, but a reasonable surplus for development is allowed.

This is why Delhi can regulate the fees of private schools (Delhi School Education Act 1973, and the Delhi School Education (Transparency in Fixation and Regulation of Fees) Act 2025) but cannot take over their management without cause.

**Art 21 and 21A.** The right to education was first read into the right to life in **Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka (1992)**. **Unni Krishnan v State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)** narrowed it: the right to free education is fundamental **only up to the age of 14**; beyond that it depends on the State's economic capacity under Art 41 and 45. Parliament then wrote **Art 21A** in 2002 (Section 4 below).

**Art 24.** No child **below 14** may be employed in a factory, mine or any other hazardous employment. It is a Fundamental Right, not a directive. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act gives it teeth. If a Vice Principal sees a Class 7 student missing school to work in a workshop, that is an Art 24 violation, not merely an attendance problem.

**Art 25 to 28: religion in school.**
- **Art 28(1)**: no religious instruction in an institution **wholly maintained out of State funds**.
- **Art 28(2)**: the exception is an institution administered by the State but set up under an endowment or trust that requires religious instruction.
- **Art 28(3)**: in an institution **recognised by or aided by the State**, nobody can be made to attend religious instruction or worship without consent; for a minor, the **guardian's** consent is needed.

In **Aruna Roy (2002)** the Court held that teaching *about* religions as part of value education is not "religious instruction". A Delhi government school is wholly State-funded, so it may teach comparative religion in a moral-science period but may not give instruction in one faith.

**Art 29 and 30: minorities.**
- **Art 29(1)**: any section of citizens with a distinct **language, script or culture** has the right to conserve it.
- **Art 29(2)**: no citizen may be denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided institution **only** on grounds of **religion, race, caste, language** or any of them.
- **Art 30(1)**: all **religious or linguistic** minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
- **Art 30(1A)**, inserted by the **44th Amendment, 1978**: if a minority institution's property is acquired, the compensation fixed must not restrict or abrogate the Art 30(1) right.
- **Art 30(2)**: the State may not discriminate in giving aid.

In **St Stephen's College v University of Delhi (1992)** the Court allowed an aided minority college to reserve up to **50 per cent** of seats for its own community. Because of **Pramati (2014)**, minority schools in Delhi are outside the RTE Act, so the Directorate of Education's 25 per cent EWS/DG draw does not include them.

## 4. Article 21A and the 86th Amendment, line by line

**The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 made three changes, and all three are tested together.** Parliament passed it in 2002 (assent **12 December 2002**), but the Article came into force only on **1 April 2010**. That is the same day as the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (Act 35 of 2009)**. The gap is about seven years because Art 21A gives the right "in such manner as the State may, by law, determine", so it needed a law before it could work.

- **Art 21A (Part III)**: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of **six to fourteen years** in such manner as the State may, by law, determine."
- **Art 45 (Part IV), substituted**: "The State shall endeavour to provide **early childhood care and education** for all children until they complete the age of **six years**." The **original Art 45** asked the State to provide free and compulsory education for children up to 14 **within ten years** of 1950.
- **Art 51A(k) (Part IVA), added**: a **parent or guardian** must provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between **six and fourteen** years. It is the **eleventh** Fundamental Duty.

Memory aid: **State 6 to 14, parent 6 to 14, ECCE under 6.** The State's duty and the parent's duty cover the same age band; the directive covers the years before it.

```mermaid
timeline
  1950 : Art 45 ten-year target
  1956 : 7th Amendment, Art 350A 350B
  1976 : 42nd, education Concurrent List
  1993 : Unni Krishnan, right till 14
  2002 : 86th Amendment, Art 21A
  2010 : Art 21A and RTE in force
  2014 : Pramati, minority schools exempt
```

**What the RTE Act does with Art 21A (in brief; it has its own unit).**
- Every child aged 6 to 14 has a right to elementary education in a neighbourhood school.
- It bars capitation fees and screening.
- **Section 12(1)(c)** requires private unaided schools to admit at least **25 per cent** disadvantaged and weaker-section children at entry level.

The Supreme Court upheld this for non-minority schools in **Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012)**. In **Lucknow Public School v State of UP (28 April 2026)** it held that a school must first admit the child allotted under the quota and raise eligibility disputes afterwards, because refusal violates Art 21A.

## 5. Directive Principles for education and children

**Part IV tells the State what to aim for; Art 37 says no court can force it.** The exam contrasts these with the enforceable rights in Part III.

- **Art 37**: Part IV is **not enforceable by any court**, yet "fundamental in the governance of the country", and the State must apply it in making laws.
- **Art 39(e) and 39(f)**: the tender age of children must not be abused. Children must get opportunities to develop in freedom and dignity and be protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment. Clause (f) was recast by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
- **Art 41**: right to work, **to education** and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, within the limits of economic capacity. Unni Krishnan leaned on this for education beyond 14.
- **Art 45**: ECCE for children below six (after 2002).
- **Art 46**: promote with special care the educational and economic interests of **weaker sections, in particular SC and ST**, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation. Pre-matric and post-matric scholarships run on this directive.
- **Art 47**: raise nutrition levels and standard of living and improve public health. PM POSHAN (the mid-day meal) rests on Art 47 read with Art 21A.

Contrast pair that traps candidates: **Art 41 is "education" in the welfare sense (adult and beyond 14); Art 45 is early childhood; Art 46 is SC/ST and weaker sections.**

## 6. Fundamental Duties (Part IVA)

**Eleven duties, one Article, non-justiciable, two Amendments.**
- The **42nd Amendment, 1976** inserted Part IVA with **ten duties**, on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**.
- The **86th Amendment, 2002** added the eleventh, **51A(k)**.
- The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) worked out how to teach them in schools.

The duties that come up in education papers:

- **51A(e)**: promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
- **51A(f)**: value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
- **51A(g)**: protect and improve the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures.
- **51A(h)**: develop **scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform**.
- **51A(j)**: **strive towards excellence** in all spheres of individual and collective activity.
- **51A(k)**: parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to the child or ward aged 6 to 14.

"Paying taxes honestly" was suggested by the Swaran Singh Committee but is **not** in Art 51A. The duties apply to **citizens**, not to foreigners. No court can directly enforce them, though courts use them to interpret laws.

## 7. Language provisions a school head must know

**Part XVII (Art 343 to 351) and the Eighth Schedule decide the official language and protect linguistic minorities in schools.**

- **Art 343**: **Hindi in Devanagari** script is the official language of the Union, with the international form of Indian numerals. English was to continue for 15 years; the **Official Languages Act, 1963** continued it indefinitely.
- **Art 345**: a State legislature may adopt any language of the State. Delhi's own law, the Delhi Official Languages Act, 2000, makes Hindi the official language and Urdu and Punjabi second official languages.
- **Art 350A**: every **State and local authority** shall endeavour to provide adequate facilities for **instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage** to children of **linguistic minority groups**; the **President** may issue directions.
- **Art 350B**: a **Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities**, appointed by the **President**, reports to the President. The President has the reports laid before **each House of Parliament** and sent to the State governments concerned.
- Both 350A and 350B were inserted by the **7th Amendment, 1956** (States Reorganisation), not by the 42nd.
- **Art 351**: duty of the Union to promote the spread of Hindi, drawing on Sanskrit and the Eighth Schedule languages.
- **Eighth Schedule**: **22 languages**; 14 originally; Sindhi (21st Amendment, 1967); Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali (71st, 1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali (92nd, 2003).

## 8. Seventh Schedule: who makes law on education

**Since 1976 both Parliament and State legislatures can make laws on education, and the Centre's law wins a conflict.** Before the 42nd Amendment, "Education" was **Entry 11 of the State List**. The **42nd Amendment Act, 1976** deleted it and placed **Entry 25 in List III (Concurrent)**: "Education, including technical education, medical education and universities, subject to the provisions of entries 63, 64, 65 and 66 of List I; vocational and technical training of labour."

Entry 25 is subject to these Union List entries:

| Entry (List I) | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **63** | Institutions of national importance named in the Constitution: **BHU, AMU, Delhi University**, plus any Parliament declares |
| **64** | Scientific or technical institutions financed by the Union and declared of national importance (IITs, for example) |
| **65** | Union agencies for professional, vocational or technical training, including police training |
| **66** | **Coordination and determination of standards** in higher education, research, scientific and technical institutions (the basis of the UGC Act, AICTE Act, NCTE Act) |

The same 42nd Amendment moved **five** subjects to the Concurrent List: **education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice (constitution of courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts)**. Public health stayed in the State List (Entry 6).

**Art 254 settles conflicts.**
- If a State law on a Concurrent subject is repugnant to a Central law, the **Central law prevails**.
- A State law reserved for the President and given assent prevails in that State, but Parliament may still override it.

So the RTE Act, 2009 (Centre) and the Delhi School Education Act, 1973 (Delhi) both operate, and where they clash the RTE Act governs. The Delhi Assembly gets its power over education through **Art 239AA(3)(a)**, which lets it make laws on Concurrent List matters applicable to Union Territories.

**Local bodies.**
- The **73rd Amendment, 1992** added Part IX and the **Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)** for Panchayats. Items **17 to 21** cover education (including primary and secondary schools), technical training and vocational education, adult and non-formal education, libraries, and cultural activities.
- The **74th Amendment, 1992** added Part IXA and the **Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects)** for Municipalities, including promotion of cultural, educational and aesthetic aspects.

In Delhi, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi runs most primary schools, and the Directorate of Education runs government schools mainly from Class 6 to 12 (Sarvodaya Vidyalayas also have primary classes). The NDMC and the Delhi Cantonment Board run their own schools.

The **106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam)** is the latest enacted amendment this pack can confirm. When this was written, two Bills were pending before Joint Parliamentary Committees:
- the **Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024** on simultaneous elections;
- the **Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025** on removing ministers who are detained for 30 days.

Check before the exam whether either has been enacted. If so, the count moves past 106.

## 10. Landmark cases in order

**Seven judgments explain how a directive became a right and where private and minority schools stand.** Learn them as a story, not a list.

1. **Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka (1992)**: right to education flows from Art 21; **capitation fee violates Art 14**.
2. **Unni Krishnan v State of AP (1993, 5 judges)**: right to free education is fundamental **only till 14**; after that it depends on economic capacity (Art 41). It also devised a "free seat and payment seat" scheme for professional colleges.
3. **T.M.A. Pai Foundation v State of Karnataka (2002, 11 judges)**: education is an "occupation" under Art 19(1)(g). It scrapped the Unni Krishnan seat scheme and held that minority status is decided State by State. No capitation fees and no profiteering, but a reasonable surplus is allowed.
4. **P.A. Inamdar v State of Maharashtra (2005, 7 judges)**: the State cannot impose its reservation policy on **unaided** private professional institutions, minority or not. Parliament answered with the **93rd Amendment** and Art 15(5).
5. **Ashoka Kumar Thakur v Union of India (2008)**: upheld the 93rd Amendment and the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 for State and aided institutions, with 27 per cent OBC reservation excluding the creamy layer.
6. **Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v Union of India (2012)**: the RTE Act and its 25 per cent quota are valid for government, aided and **unaided non-minority** schools; unaided minority schools are exempt.
7. **Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v Union of India (2014, 5 judges)**: Art 15(5) and Art 21A are constitutionally valid; the RTE Act does **not** apply to **minority schools, aided or unaided**, because of Art 30(1).

Other cases cited in education papers:
- **Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: students who stood silently during the National Anthem could not be expelled (Art 19(1)(a) and 25).
- **Avinash Mehrotra (2009)**: read fire-safety norms for schools into Art 21A.
- **Dr Jaya Thakur v Union of India (30 January 2026)**: menstrual health is part of Art 21, linked to Art 21A. The Court ordered free sanitary pads and working separate toilets for girls in Classes 6 to 12.

## 11. Delhi's constitutional position

**Delhi is a Union Territory with a Legislative Assembly under Art 239AA, and three subjects stay with the Union.**
- Delhi was a Part C State, with an elected Assembly from 1952 to 1956, and became a Union Territory on **1 November 1956**.
- It got its present shape through the **69th Amendment Act, 1991** (in force **1 February 1992**). This inserted **Art 239AA** and **239AB** and renamed it the **National Capital Territory of Delhi**.
- The **GNCTD Act, 1991** fills in the detail; the first Assembly was elected in **1993**.

- **Assembly**: **70 members**, all directly elected. It may legislate on State List and Concurrent List matters applicable to UTs, **except Entries 1 (public order), 2 (police) and 18 (land)** of the State List (Art 239AA(3)(a)).
- **Repugnancy**: if an Assembly law conflicts with a law of Parliament, **Parliament's law prevails** (Art 239AA(3)(c)), subject to the Presidential-assent proviso.
- **Council of Ministers**: **not more than 10 per cent** of the Assembly, so **7 including the Chief Minister** (Art 239AA(4)). It aids and advises the Lieutenant Governor; a difference of opinion goes to the **President**.
- **Chief Minister** is appointed by the **President**, and other ministers by the President on the CM's advice (Art 239AA(5)); they are collectively responsible to the Assembly (Art 239AA(6)).
- **Lieutenant Governor** is the Administrator under **Art 239**. **Delhi Police** reports to the Union Home Ministry.
- **70th Amendment Act, 1992** amended **Art 54** so that elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry vote for the **President of India**.
- Delhi sends **7 members to the Lok Sabha** and **3 to the Rajya Sabha**; the **Delhi High Court** dates from **31 October 1966**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  PR[President of India] --> LG[Lieutenant Governor, Art 239]
  PR --> CM[Chief Minister appointed]
  CM --> COM[Council of Ministers, max 7]
  COM --> LA[Legislative Assembly, 70 MLAs]
  LA --> ST[State and Concurrent subjects]
  PAR[Parliament] --> EX[Police, public order, land]
```

**The services dispute, step by step.**
- **July 2018**: a five-judge bench held that the LG is bound by the aid and advice of the ministers and has no independent decision-making power. His only option is to refer a difference of opinion to the President under the Art 239AA(4) proviso.
- **11 May 2023**: another Constitution Bench held that "services" fall under the Delhi government, except where they relate to public order, police and land.
- **GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023**: Parliament then created the **National Capital Civil Service Authority** to recommend transfers and postings. The Chief Minister chairs it, with the Chief Secretary and the Principal Home Secretary as members, and the LG's decision is final if they differ. The Act was challenged in the Supreme Court.
- **GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2021**: earlier, this had declared that "Government" in laws passed by the Assembly means the LG.

**Who holds office (per the knowledge base, as of October 2026).** Chief Minister **Rekha Gupta** and Education Minister **Ashish Sood**, both since **February 2025**. **V.K. Saxena** was appointed Lieutenant Governor in May 2022. The knowledge base does not confirm the current holder, so check before the exam.

## 12. Constitutional current affairs, October 2025 to October 2026

**The live items are appointments, a Presidential reference and two rulings on Art 21A.**

- **Justice Surya Kant** became the **53rd Chief Justice of India on 24 November 2025**, succeeding Justice B.R. Gavai; he retires on 9 February 2027.
- **C.P. Radhakrishnan** was elected **Vice-President** in **September 2025** after Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned in July 2025 under **Art 67(a)**.
- **President Droupadi Murmu** has held office since July 2022; the next Presidential election is due in 2027.
- **Governor's assent**: in April 2025 the Supreme Court set timelines for Governors under Art 200 in the Tamil Nadu case. The President then sought the Court's opinion under **Art 143**. In November 2025 a Constitution Bench said courts cannot fix such timelines or grant "deemed assent".
- **Dr Jaya Thakur (30 January 2026)**: menstrual health under Art 21, read with Art 21A.
- **Lucknow Public School v State of UP (28 April 2026)**: admit RTE-quota children first, dispute eligibility later.
- **Census 2027** (reference date 1 March 2027) is the "first Census after commencement" that triggers delimitation and the women's reservation under the **106th Amendment**.
- **Union Education Minister**: Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on 25 July 2026 and **Pralhad Joshi** holds additional charge, as reported in the news. The President accepted the resignation under **Art 75(2)**. Check whether a full-time minister has been named since.

## Common traps

- **86th versus 93rd versus 42nd**: 86th = Art 21A (2002); 93rd = Art 15(5) (2005); 42nd = Concurrent List and duties (1976). The 44th gave Art 30(1A), not 21A.
- **Part placement**: Art 21A is Part III; Art 45 is Part IV; Art 51A(k) is Part IVA. "Art 21A is a Directive Principle" is always false.
- **Who is bound**: Art 21A binds the **State**; Art 51A(k) binds the **parent or guardian**; Art 350A binds **State and local authority**.
- **Age bands**: Art 21A and 51A(k) are **6 to 14**; new Art 45 is **below 6**; Art 24 is **below 14**; RPwD Act free education is **6 to 18**.
- **Dates**: 86th Amendment assent **12 December 2002**; Art 21A in force **1 April 2010**. An option saying "in force 2002" is wrong.
- **Art 28**: wholly State-funded means **no** religious instruction; recognised or aided means **consent** needed. Statement writers swap these.
- **Art 29(2)** lists religion, race, caste, **language**; it does not say "sex" or "place of birth" (those are in Art 15(1)).
- **Entry 25 List III** (education) versus **Entry 66 List I** (standards in higher education) versus **Entry 63 List I** (BHU, AMU, DU).
- **42nd Amendment shifts**: education, forests, wildlife, weights and measures, administration of justice. **Not** public health, not agriculture, not police.
- **Cases**: Mohini Jain (1992) came **before** Unni Krishnan (1993); Pai (2002) **before** Inamdar (2005). Rajasthan Schools (2012) exempted only **unaided** minority schools; Pramati (2014) exempted **all** minority schools, aided or unaided.
- **Delhi**: 69th Amendment created the Assembly; **70th** put Delhi MLAs in the Presidential electoral college; CM is appointed by the **President**, not the LG; ministers **7**, not 10 or 12; Rajya Sabha **3**, not 5.
- **Fundamental Duties**: eleven, not ten; no duty to pay taxes or to vote.

## Remember for the exam

1. Art 21A: 86th Amendment 2002, in force 1 April 2010, ages 6 to 14, Part III, "in such manner as the State may, by law, determine".
2. New Art 45: ECCE until six; original Art 45: free and compulsory education up to 14 within ten years.
3. Art 51A(k): parent or guardian, 6 to 14, eleventh duty; first ten by the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice.
4. Art 37: Directive Principles not enforceable by any court.
5. Art 28(1) no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions; 28(3) consent in recognised or aided ones.
6. Art 29(2): no denial of admission only on religion, race, caste, language; Art 30(1): religious or linguistic minorities; 30(1A) by the 44th Amendment 1978.
7. Art 15(4) 1st Amendment 1951; 15(5) 93rd Amendment 2005; 15(6) and 16(6) 103rd Amendment 2019 (10 per cent EWS, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan 2022).
8. Art 41 work, education, public assistance; Art 46 SC, ST, weaker sections; Art 47 nutrition and public health; Art 24 no child under 14 in hazardous work.
9. Art 350A mother-tongue instruction at primary stage; Art 350B Special Officer appointed by the President; both by the 7th Amendment 1956.
10. 42nd Amendment 1976: education from State List Entry 11 to Concurrent List Entry 25; Union List Entry 66 standards in higher education; Entry 63 BHU, AMU, DU.
11. Eleventh Schedule 29 subjects (items 17 to 21 education-related); Twelfth Schedule 18 subjects.
12. Mohini Jain 1992, Unni Krishnan 1993, T.M.A. Pai 2002, Inamdar 2005, Ashoka Kumar Thakur 2008, Rajasthan Schools 2012, Pramati 2014.
13. Delhi: 69th Amendment 1991 (in force 1 Feb 1992), Art 239AA, 70 MLAs, 7 ministers, no power over public order, police, land; 70th Amendment 1992 for the Presidential electoral college.
14. GNCTD (Amendment) Act 2023 created the National Capital Civil Service Authority after the 11 May 2023 judgment on services.
15. Current: CJI Surya Kant (53rd, 24 Nov 2025); Vice-President C.P. Radhakrishnan (Sept 2025); 106th Amendment 2023 is the latest confirmed amendment.

- Knowledge base: units/gk.md (Static GK notes, 2026); research/02-child-rights-law.md; research/05-current-affairs.md (digest Oct 2025 to Oct 2026, compiled 9 Oct 2026).
- M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity (chapters on Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties, Union Territories), for structure and amendment history.
quick_facts: Art 21A (86th Amendment, 2002; in force 1 April 2010): free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14, in Part III, enforceable in court.
New Art 45 (Part IV): early childhood care and education until age six; the original Art 45 set a ten-year target for free education up to 14.
Art 51A(k): the parent or guardian must provide education opportunities to the child or ward aged 6 to 14; it is the eleventh Fundamental Duty.
Art 37: Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court but are fundamental in governance.
Art 28(1): no religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained from State funds; Art 28(3): consent (guardian's for minors) needed in recognised or aided institutions.
Art 29(2) bars denial of admission only on religion, race, caste or language; Art 30(1) protects religious and linguistic minorities; Art 30(1A) came by the 44th Amendment, 1978.
Art 15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005) allows reservation in private aided and unaided institutions except minority ones; it answered the Inamdar judgment of 2005.
42nd Amendment, 1976 moved education from State List Entry 11 to Concurrent List Entry 25; Union List Entry 66 covers standards in higher education.
Art 350A (mother-tongue instruction at primary stage) and Art 350B (Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities, appointed by the President) were inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
Case order: Mohini Jain 1992, Unni Krishnan 1993 (right till 14), T.M.A. Pai 2002, Inamdar 2005, Rajasthan Schools 2012, Pramati 2014 (RTE Act does not apply to minority schools).
Eleventh Schedule (73rd Amendment) has 29 Panchayat subjects including primary and secondary schools; Twelfth Schedule (74th Amendment) has 18.
Delhi: 69th Amendment 1991 inserted Art 239AA; 70 MLAs; Council of Ministers at most 10 per cent (7); no power over public order, police and land; CM appointed by the President.
70th Amendment 1992 added Delhi and Puducherry MLAs to the electoral college for the President of India.
GNCTD (Amendment) Act 2023 created the National Capital Civil Service Authority after the Supreme Court's 11 May 2023 ruling that services vest in the Delhi government.
Current: Justice Surya Kant is the 53rd CJI (24 Nov 2025); C.P. Radhakrishnan is Vice-President (Sept 2025); the 106th Amendment (2023) is the latest confirmed amendment.

mcqs.q_en: Which Article of the Constitution declares that the Directive Principles of State Policy shall not be enforceable by any court, though they are fundamental in the governance of the country?
mcqs.explain_en: Art 37 makes Part IV non-justiciable while directing the State to apply the principles in making laws. Art 36 only defines 'State' for Part IV, Art 38 is the directive on social order, and Art 51 concerns international peace.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Part IV, Art 37

mcqs.q_en:
With reference to Article 28 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds.
2. This bar applies even to an institution administered by the State but established under an endowment or trust that requires religious instruction to be imparted.
3. In an institution recognised by the State or receiving State aid, a minor may be made to attend religious instruction only if his guardian has consented.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcqs.explain_en: Statement 1 is Art 28(1) and statement 3 is Art 28(3), so both are correct. Statement 2 is wrong because Art 28(2) expressly exempts an institution administered by the State but established under an endowment or trust that requires religious instruction.

mcqs.q_en:
Match List I (Entry) with List II (Subject) and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List I
A. Entry 25, List III (Concurrent List)
B. Entry 66, List I (Union List)
C. Entry 63, List I (Union List)
D. Entry 17, Eleventh Schedule
List II
1. Institutions of national importance such as BHU, AMU and the University of Delhi
2. Education, including technical education, medical education and universities
3. Coordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education or research
4. Education, including primary and secondary schools (a Panchayat subject)
mcqs.explain_en: Entry 25 of List III has been the general education entry since 1976. Entry 66 of List I is the standards entry under which the UGC, AICTE and NCTE laws are made. Entry 63 names BHU, AMU and Delhi University. Item 17 of the Eleventh Schedule gives Panchayats primary and secondary schools. The wrong options swap Entries 63 and 66 or the Eleventh Schedule item.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule List I Entries 63 and 66, List III Entry 25; Eleventh Schedule item 17

mcqs.q_en:
Assertion (A): A child denied free elementary education can seek enforcement of Article 21A in a court, but a parent cannot compel the State through a court to provide early childhood care under Article 45.
Reason (R): Article 21A is in Part III of the Constitution, whereas Article 45 is in Part IV, whose provisions Article 37 declares to be not enforceable by any court.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
options_en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explain_en: Both statements are true, and R is exactly why A holds: Fundamental Rights in Part III can be enforced in court, while Art 37 bars courts from enforcing the Directive Principles in Part IV. The trap is to treat both Articles as equally enforceable because both concern education.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Art 21A (Part III), Art 37 and Art 45 (Part IV)

mcqs.q_en:
Arrange the following Supreme Court judgments on education in chronological order (earliest first):
1. T.M.A. Pai Foundation v State of Karnataka
2. Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka
3. Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v Union of India
4. Unni Krishnan v State of Andhra Pradesh
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
mcqs.explain_en:
The order is:
- Mohini Jain (1992) first read education into Art 21.
- Unni Krishnan (1993) limited the right to age 14.
- T.M.A. Pai (2002) treated education as an occupation under Art 19(1)(g).
- Pramati (2014) exempted minority schools from the RTE Act.
Option A swaps the first two, which is the commonest error.
mcqs.source: Supreme Court: Mohini Jain (1992), Unni Krishnan (1993), T.M.A. Pai (2002), Pramati (2014)

mcqs.q_en:
Consider the following statements about Article 45 of the Constitution:
1. As originally enacted, it directed the State to endeavour to provide, within ten years of the commencement of the Constitution, free and compulsory education for all children until they complete fourteen years.
2. As substituted by the 86th Amendment, it directs the State to endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years.
3. Being a Directive Principle, it can be enforced by a writ in the High Court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcqs.explain_en: Statements 1 and 2 correctly give the text of Art 45 before and after 2002. Statement 3 is wrong because Art 37 makes Directive Principles non-enforceable; the enforceable right for ages 6 to 14 is Art 21A.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Art 45 (original and as substituted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002); Art 37

mcqs.q_en: In Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v Union of India (2014), a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that:
options_en: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 applies to unaided minority schools but not to aided minority schools
Article 15(5), inserted by the 93rd Amendment, is unconstitutional as it violates the basic structure
the RTE Act, 2009 does not apply to minority schools, whether aided or unaided, while Article 15(5) and Article 21A are constitutionally valid
the 25 per cent quota under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act applies only to Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas
mcqs.explain_en: Pramati upheld the 93rd Amendment (Art 15(5)) and the 86th Amendment (Art 21A). It also held that the RTE Act is ultra vires Art 30(1) to the extent it applies to minority schools, aided or unaided. Option A is wrong: no judgment held this. The 2012 Rajasthan Schools judgment said the reverse, exempting only unaided minority schools, and Pramati widened that exemption to aided minority schools as well.
mcqs.source: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v Union of India, Supreme Court, 6 May 2014; Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012)

mcqs.q_en: The Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities under Article 350B of the Constitution is appointed by:
options_en: the Chairman of the National Commission for Minorities
mcqs.explain_en: Art 350B(1) provides for a Special Officer appointed by the President, who reports to the President. The reports are laid before each House of Parliament and sent to the States concerned. The Article was inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Art 350B; Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956

mcqs.q_en:
With reference to the National Capital Territory of Delhi under Article 239AA, consider the following statements:
1. The Council of Ministers shall not exceed ten per cent of the total number of members in the Legislative Assembly.
2. The Chief Minister of Delhi is appointed by the Lieutenant Governor.
3. Where a law made by the Legislative Assembly of Delhi is repugnant to a law made by Parliament, the law made by Parliament prevails.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcqs.explain_en: Art 239AA(4) caps the Council of Ministers at 10 per cent of the Assembly (7 ministers), and Art 239AA(3)(c) gives Parliament's law priority. Statement 2 is wrong: under Art 239AA(5) the Chief Minister is appointed by the President, not by the Lieutenant Governor.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Art 239AA(3)(c), (4), (5); Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991

mcqs.q_en: The Constitution (Ninety-third Amendment) Act, 2005, which inserted Article 15(5) to enable reservation in admissions to private educational institutions, was enacted mainly in response to which Supreme Court judgment?
options_en: Mohini Jain v State of Karnataka (1992)
Unni Krishnan v State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)
P.A. Inamdar v State of Maharashtra (2005)
Ashoka Kumar Thakur v Union of India (2008)
mcqs.explain_en: In August 2005 a seven-judge bench in Inamdar held that the State could not impose its reservation policy on unaided private institutions, and within months Parliament responded with Art 15(5). Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) came later and upheld the amendment, so it cannot be the cause.
mcqs.source: P.A. Inamdar v State of Maharashtra (2005); Constitution (Ninety-third Amendment) Act, 2005; Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)

mcqs.q_en: Which one of the following subjects was NOT transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976?
options_en: Weights and measures (except establishment of standards)
Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries
mcqs.explain_en:
The 42nd Amendment moved five subjects to List III:
- education
- forests
- protection of wild animals and birds
- weights and measures
- administration of justice (courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts)

Public health and sanitation is still Entry 6 of the State List.
mcqs.source: Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976; Seventh Schedule, List II Entry 6, List III Entries 11A, 17A, 17B, 25, 33A

mcqs.q_en: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty listed in Article 51A of the Constitution?
options_en: To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
To pay taxes honestly and on time
To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity
For a parent or guardian, to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years
mcqs.explain_en: Art 51A lists eleven duties, including (h) scientific temper, (j) striving for excellence and (k) the parent's duty. The Swaran Singh Committee suggested a duty to pay taxes, but it was never included in Part IVA.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Part IVA, Art 51A(a) to (k); Swaran Singh Committee recommendations, 1976

mcqs.q_en:
Match List I (Article) with List II (Directive) and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List I
A. Article 41
B. Article 45
C. Article 46
D. Article 47
List II
1. Raising the level of nutrition and the standard of living and improving public health
2. Early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years
3. Right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement
4. Promotion of the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
mcqs.explain_en:
The correct matches are:
- Art 41: work, education and public assistance (welfare directive)
- Art 45 (since 2002): ECCE for children below six
- Art 46: SC, ST and weaker sections
- Art 47: nutrition and public health

Option C swaps Arts 46 and 47, the pair most often confused.
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Part IV, Arts 41, 45, 46, 47

mcqs.q_en:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under Article 29(2), no citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.
2. The right under Article 30(1) to establish and administer educational institutions is available to both religious and linguistic minorities.
3. Article 30(1A), which protects minority institutions in matters of compensation on compulsory acquisition of their property, was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcqs.explain_en: Statements 1 and 2 correctly state Art 29(2) and Art 30(1). Statement 3 is wrong because Art 30(1A) was inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978; the 86th Amendment dealt with Arts 21A, 45 and 51A(k).
mcqs.source: Constitution of India, Arts 29(2), 30(1), 30(1A); Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978

mcqs.q_en: In Unni Krishnan v State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), the Supreme Court held that:
options_en: the right to education at all levels, including professional education, is a Fundamental Right under Article 21
the right to free education is a Fundamental Right flowing from Article 21 only until a child completes fourteen years; beyond that it is subject to the limits of the State's economic capacity
running an educational institution is a 'trade' and cannot be regulated by the State
charging capitation fee is permissible if the institution is unaided
mcqs.explain_en: Unni Krishnan read the right to education into Art 21 but, drawing on Arts 41 and 45, limited the right to free education to age 14. Education beyond that depends on the State's economic capacity. This narrowed the broad view in Mohini Jain (option A). The Court also did not allow capitation fees and did not treat education as a trade.
mcqs.source: Unni Krishnan v State of Andhra Pradesh, Supreme Court (1993), five-judge bench; Arts 21, 41, 45

changes: All 15 answer keys checked by solving each question first; no key was wrong.

Q7 explanation: it said option A 'describes the 2012 Rajasthan Schools position', which is wrong. Rajasthan Schools (2012) exempted only unaided minority schools, the reverse of option A; Pramati extended the exemption to aided minority schools too.
Q6 statement 1: 'directed the State to provide' → 'directed the State to endeavour to provide', matching the original Art 45 wording. Key unchanged.

Reading §2: removed the claim that a Delhi government teacher's termination case goes straight to the High Court under Art 226 'because service matters are not Fundamental Rights'. GNCTD employees go first to the Central Administrative Tribunal, then to the High Court under Art 226 (L. Chandra Kumar 1997). Added that Art 32 enforces Fundamental Rights only.

Reading §3: 'Nine Articles of Part III' → 'About a dozen' (the section covers Arts 14, 15, 16, 19, 21, 21A, 24, 25–28, 29, 30). Gave the full name of the Delhi Fee Regulation Act 2025, as in units/gk.md.
Reading §4: 'eight-year gap' → 'about seven years' (assent 12 Dec 2002 to commencement 1 Apr 2010).

Reading §8: 'DoE runs classes 6 to 12' → 'mainly Class 6 to 12', with a note that Sarvodaya Vidyalayas have primary classes and that the NDMC and Cantonment Board run schools. Removed the unsourced claim that the RTE Act's local-authority duties fall on the MCD.
Reading §9 table: the 106th Amendment also reserves one-third of seats in the Delhi Legislative Assembly (it amended Art 239AA), not only in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
Reading §10: 'Six judgments' → 'Seven judgments'; the section lists seven.

Reading §11: 'Part C State from 1952 to 1956' → Part C State with an elected Assembly from 1952 to 1956 (Delhi was a Part C State from 1950). 2018 judgment: added that the LG can only refer a difference of opinion to the President under the Art 239AA(4) proviso.
